name: Ramp
text: Add one high-contrast skip link at the very top of every page that jumps straight to `<main role="main">` and keep it visible at all times. This fixes keyboard navigation for screen reader users and power users who rely on skip links, without cluttering the interface. The trade-off is a small permanent element that may slightly reduce screen real estate, but the accessibility win outweighs this cost.

name: Reader
text: A single high-contrast skip link fails users who rely on screen readers when the `<main role="main">` is dynamically updated or injected after page load—like in SPAs or lazy-loaded content. Instead, pair it with a **programmatic focus trap** that forces focus into `<main>` on route changes, ensuring every user lands where they expect. Test with a screen reader: if focus doesn’t auto-shift to `<main>` after dynamic updates, the skip link alone isn’t enough.

name: Ramp
text:
Add a **programmatic focus trap** that forces focus into `<main role="main">` on every route change or dynamic content injection. This guarantees screen reader users land in the main content immediately, even when the DOM updates after page load—fixing the failure case of a static skip link. The trade-off is a small JavaScript dependency and potential focus flicker, but it’s the only way to ensure reliability across all navigation patterns.

name: Reader
text: Forcing focus into `<main role="main">` on every route change can be jarring for users who rely on screen readers, as it disrupts their expected navigation flow. A better approach might be to use a more nuanced focus management strategy, such as announces when the main content changes, allowing users to opt-in to navigating the updated content. This argument would be settled by user testing with screen reader users to determine the most effective and least disruptive approach.
